docs.title: aibi-dax
docs.text: dxa — DAX expression analysis: complexity metrics, anti-pattern detection and per-model ranking. Companion to aibi-toolkit: where the toolkit checks the model around your measures (naming, formats, hygiene), aibi-dax checks the expressions inside them.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
pip install .
dxa --version

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command Purpose dxa metrics "EXPR" six complexity metrics plus a single weighted score (--file) dxa rank model.json --top N the most complex measures of a model dump (--min-weight W) dxa lint "EXPR" anti-pattern findings for one expression (--rule, --list-rules [--json], --file) dxa explain RULE full documentation for one anti-pattern rule (--json) dxa lint-model model.json findings across every measure, grouped (--table, --rule, --summary) dxa parse "EXPR" the recursive-descent AST, human or --json (--file)

docs.title: The weight
docs.text:
weight = tokens + 3·functions + 5·depth + 20·iterators — iterators cost the most because row context is where DAX quietly goes wrong.

See the seventeen anti-pattern rules for what the linter flags and why.

docs.title: Global
docs.text:
dxa --version        # dxa 0.2.1
dxa --help

docs.title: dxa metrics "EXPR"
docs.text:
Prints six aligned metrics plus the composite weight:

$ dxa metrics "SUMX('Sales', CALCULATE([Amount]))"
tokens      9
lines       1
chars       34
functions   2
depth       2
iterators   1
weight      45

--json wraps the same payload: {"metrics": {...}, "weight": 45}. --file PATH reads the expression from a file (- for stdin), matching dxa lint.

docs.title: dxa rank model.json [--top N] [--min-weight W]
docs.text:
Weighs every measure in a shared-schema model dump:

$ dxa rank model.json --top 3
    57  Sales.Iterator Calc
    34  Sales.If Stair
    12  Sales.Clean Total

--min-weight 40 keeps only measures at or above that weight, which is the review question "what crosses the line"; --top N then applies to the filtered set. It composes with --table and --json.

docs.title: dxa lint "EXPR"
docs.text:
Anti-pattern findings for one expression. Exit code 0 when clean, 1 with - lines per finding. --json prints the findings as a JSON list ([] when clean). --rule NAME runs a single rule (function name, exit 2 with the rule list on stderr if unknown). --list-rules prints the rule inventory with each rule's summary and exits 0. --list-rules --json prints that inventory as [{"name": …, "summary": …}] for editor plugins and CI allow-lists. --file PATH reads the expression from a file instead, so a measure copied from a model keeps its newlines and quotes; --file - reads stdin, so cat measure.dax | dxa lint --file - works in a pipeline. Pass one source or the other, never both. A blank expression — nothing, or only whitespace, from any source — exits 2 with got an empty expression from … rather than passing silently:

$ dxa lint "IF(a, 1, IF(b, 2, IF(c, 3, [D]/[E])))"
- 3 nested IF calls — SWITCH(TRUE(), ...) reads better and evaluates faster.
- Raw '/' division — use DIVIDE(num, den) to absorb zero-denominator errors.
(exit 1)

docs.title: dxa explain RULE
docs.text:
Full documentation for one rule — its docstring, underlined. Exit 2 with the complete rule list on stderr if the name is unknown. Names match case-insensitively and ignore surrounding whitespace; the heading always prints the canonical lower-case name. --json emits {"name", "summary", "doc"} — the same summary as --list-rules --json and the docstring without the heading, for editor hovers:

$ dxa explain earlier_var
earlier_var
-----------
EARLIER is superseded by VAR capture — flat and type-checkable.

docs.title: dxa lint-model model.json
docs.text:
Groups findings by table.measure; --table T restricts to one table. --rule NAME runs a single rule (function name, exit 2 with the rule list on stderr if unknown). Prints nothing and exits 0 for a clean model. Findings exit 1 with - lines per finding; --json prints the findings map.

--summary swaps the per-measure listing for a model-wide rule histogram — the count of measures each rule fires on, heaviest first. It respects --table and --rule, and --json emits the counts as an object. Exit 1 when anything fires, 0 with model is clean otherwise:

$ dxa lint-model model.json --summary
    2  calculate_inside_iterator
    1  raw_division

docs.title: dxa parse "EXPR"
docs.text:
Reduces the expression to an AST (recursive descent; exit 2 on a genuinely unparseable sequence). --json prints the tree as JSON; --file PATH reads the expression from a file instead of the command line (- for stdin), so multiline measures keep their shape. --tree prints it one node per line, children indented, with field: labels where position alone would not say what the child is:

$ dxa parse "1 + [A]" --tree
Binary op='+'
  left:
    Literal text='1'
  right:
    ColumnRef name='A'

$ dxa parse "1 + [A]" --json
{
  "op": "+",
  "left": {
    "text": "1"
  },
  "right": {
    "name": "A"
  }
}

Unparseable sequences exit 2 with a parse error: message on stderr. A missing quote or bracket names the delimiter and where it opened (unterminated string starting at char 4), and doubled delimiters are escapes, not closers ("a""b", 'T''x', [A]]]]]).

The grammar covers VAR … RETURN blocks, calls, qualified columns, list literals, and the operator ladder ||, &&, comparison/IN, + -, &, * /, unary. IN binds with the comparisons, and its right side is usually a list. Unary operators are - + ! and the keyword NOT (either case), so NOT ISBLANK([x]), NOT ([a] = 1) and [a] && NOT [b] parse. Table qualifiers may be quoted or bare ('Sales'[Amount], Sales[Amount]):

$ dxa parse "[k] IN {1, 2}" --tree
Binary op='IN'
  left:
    ColumnRef name='k'
  right:
    List
      Literal text='1'
      Literal text='2'

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: The linter is designed for interactive use: dxa lint-model runs in milliseconds over realistic dumps, so nothing here needs caching, threading, or a server. This page records what each stage costs and how the numbers are produced.

docs.title: Corpus
docs.text:
examples/bench_rules.py defines a 22-expression corpus covering every rule's positive and negative form — plain aggregates, division shapes, BLANK comparisons, IF/SWITCH stairs, iterators (nested and single-column), VAR blocks, ALL filters, IFERROR, EARLIER, and lowercase calls. The model benchmark instantiates the corpus four times as tables T0..T3.

Reproduce with:

python examples/bench_rules.py

docs.title: Per-rule cost
docs.text:
Mean time per expression per rule, 50 rounds over the corpus (macOS, CPython 3.12, aibi-dax 0.2.1):

Rule µs/expr calculate_inside_iterator 2.4 raw_division 3.2 lowercase_function 1.9 too_many_ifs 1.7 single_column_iterator 1.7 concat_ampersand 1.7 bare_all_table 1.7 iferror_overuse 1.7 nested_iterators 1.7 blank_comparison 1.6 switch_missing_default 1.5 all_first_argument 1.2 earlier_var 0.9 values_with_hasonevalue 0.4

docs.title: Pipeline cost
docs.text:
Stage Before memoization Current lint_expression 202 µs/expr 25 µs/expr lint_model 17.8 ms/model 2.2 ms/model

The ~8× gain comes from one change: parse() is memoized (lru_cache, 512 entries). Every AST-driven rule parses the expression it inspects, so without the cache one lint_expression call reparsed the same string once per rule. Trees are frozen dataclasses, so sharing them across rules and calls is safe.

docs.title: Notes for contributors
docs.text:
• Bench numbers are machine-dependent; treat tables here as relative comparisons, not absolute promises.
  • Add the corpus form for any new rule to CORPUS in examples/bench_rules.py and re-run the bench before adding a row here.
  • The docs smoke tests pin CLI output, not performance numbers — timing drift alone will not fail CI, but a large regression should open an issue rather than a silent docs edit.

docs.title: DAX anti-patterns — the reference
docs.text: Each rule shipped by dxa lint with its reasoning and a fix. Community DAX guidance (SQLBI, DAX Guide) is the common source of truth; the engine here flags the pattern and the message names the preferred form.

docs.title: CALCULATE inside an iterator
docs.text: SUMX('Sales', CALCULATE([Amount])) — the iterator's row context shadows the filter context CALCULATE would use, so the result rarely matches intent. Hoist CALCULATE outside or pass explicit filters.

docs.title: EARLIER(...)
docs.text: Deprecated since VAR became the idiomatic way to capture an outer row. Capture once, reference by name — it type-checks and stays readable.

docs.title: ALL / FILTER(ALL(...)) as an aggregate's first argument
docs.text: SUMX(ALL('Sales'), ...) walks every row through the filter machinery. A boolean filter ('Sales'[Col] = value) inside CALCULATE prunes the table during scan instead of after.

docs.title: FILTER inside an aggregate
docs.text: COUNTROWS(FILTER('Sales', cond)) and SUMX(FILTER('Sales', cond), …) build a filtered table in memory before aggregating. The same condition as a CALCULATE filter is pushed into the scan: CALCULATE(COUNTROWS('Sales'), cond). Only the aggregate's first argument is checked, so FILTER used elsewhere — a CALCULATE filter argument, a nested step — stays silent.

docs.title: Three or more IF calls
docs.text: SWITCH(TRUE(), cond, value, ...) states a decision table rather than a staircase, and evaluates each branch once.

docs.title: IFERROR overreach
docs.text: IFERROR(expr, blank) turns any failure into silence — including bugs. Prefer DIVIDE's third argument, or fix what raises.

docs.title: HASONEVALUE + VALUES pairs
docs.text: IF(HASONEVALUE(k), VALUES(k), other) is exactly SELECTEDVALUE(k, other).

docs.title: SWITCH without a default
docs.text: SWITCH(expr, v1, r1, v2, r2) returns BLANK when nothing matches — silently. The optional final argument states the miss case explicitly, even if it is 0 or an error message. The rule counts arguments on the AST: an even number after the first means no default is present.

docs.title: Single-column row iterator
docs.text: SUMX('Sales', 'Sales'[Amount]) walks the table to read one column; the plain aggregate SUM('Sales'[Amount]) is faster and identical. The rule matches the iterator's first argument against the column's table qualification on the AST, so mismatched tables stay flagged as real iteration.

docs.title: ABS against an impossible bound
docs.text: ABS(x) is never negative, so ABS(x) < 0 (and <= n for negative n, mirrored as 0 > ABS(x) / -1 >= ABS(x)) can never hold — almost always a sign slip. AST-driven: one side is a one-argument ABS call, the other a numeric literal; the always-true mirrors (ABS(x) >= 0) are legitimate defensive style and stay silent.

docs.title: IF with TRUE()/FALSE() branches
docs.text: IF(cond, TRUE(), FALSE()) computes the value the condition already is — one branch and a boolean coercion for nothing. Write cond; for the inverted IF(cond, FALSE(), TRUE()) write NOT cond. AST-driven: only a three-argument IF whose last two arguments are zero-argument TRUE() / FALSE() calls flags, so bare TRUE identifiers and two-argument IFs stay silent.

docs.title: Raw division
docs.text: / raises #NUM! on zero denominators; DIVIDE(num, den[, alt]) absorbs. AST-driven: only non-constant denominators flag — [x] / 2 is safe, [x] / [Scale] is the trap, and slashes inside string literals never count.

docs.title: = BLANK() equality
docs.text: Equality against BLANK is unreliable for non-numeric types; ISBLANK(x) is the intended test.

docs.title: Bare ALL(table)
docs.text: As a filter eraser REMOVEFILTERS(table) says exactly that; keep ALL where you need its modifying semantics.

docs.title: & inside CONCATENATEX
docs.text: Concatenate via the iterator's arguments; mixing & inside is ordering hazard with hidden separators. AST-driven: & inside a string literal is data and never flags.

docs.title: Lowercase function calls
docs.text: DAX function names are uppercase by convention — sum( is a typo until proven otherwise. Literal strings and bracketed columns are exempt.

docs.title: Nested row iterators
docs.text: SUMX('Sales', AVERAGEX('Sales', [x])) pays a context transition per row for every iterator on the path. Capture the outer step in a VAR and aggregate over it. This rule runs over the parser AST — the tree is why it knows how deep the iterators stack.
